# Results — Study 43 (Free-Lunch): betting against beta on a liquid-ETF cross-section, 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily returns of **13 liquid ETFs**
spanning the beta spectrum (XLU/XLP/XLV/TLT/IEF/GLD … XLK/XLY/XLF/XLE/XLI/IWM/EEM) with **SPY** as the
market. Beta-neutral BAB: long the low-beta half (levered to beta 1), short the high-beta half,
rebalanced monthly. As-of **2026-06-30**; inputs fingerprint `dbdf824e8421`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Free lunch"? `BUSTED`

The low-beta tilt is faintly real but **does not beat the market even gross**: BAB's gross Sharpe is
**0.47** against SPY's **0.59**. And making the spread beta-neutral requires running the long leg at
**2.78× leverage** — so once you pay to borrow it, the famous edge collapses: net Sharpe falls to
**0.20** at a realistic 3% financing rate and to **0.02** at 5%. The "low-risk anomaly that beats the
market" is `BUSTED` as a free lunch: **the lunch is the leverage bill**, exactly the mechanism Study 30
(House-Edge) found for levered dip-buying. It has also `decayed` — gross Sharpe **0.70 (1999–2012) →
0.28 (2013–on)**.

## Data stamp

- **Cross-section**: 13 ETFs + SPY, 2000-01 → 2026-06, 318 months, fingerprint `dbdf824e8421`
- **Average long-leg leverage**: 2.78×

## BAB vs the leverage bill

| | CAGR | Sharpe | vol | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BAB gross (free leverage) | +8.1% | **0.47** | 21.6% | −45% |
| BAB net (financing 3% + borrow 0.5%) | +2.0% | **0.20** | 21.6% | −54% |
| BAB net (financing 5% + borrow 1%) | −2.0% | **0.02** | 21.6% | −69% |
| **SPY (the market)** | +8.1% | **0.59** | 15.2% | −51% |

Two things at once. First, **even gross, BAB's Sharpe (0.47) is below the market's (0.59)** — on this
tradable cross-section the "anomaly" doesn't clear the simplest benchmark. Second, the leverage it
needs to be beta-neutral (2.78×) means a realistic financing rate **halves the Sharpe and then erases
it**: at 5%, BAB compounds *negatively*. The headline number lives entirely in the free-leverage
assumption.

## Why the leverage is the whole story

The low-beta leg has β ≈ 0.36, so it must be held at **1/0.36 ≈ 2.8×** to reach beta 1. Frazzini &
Pedersen's thesis is that leverage-constrained investors *bid up* high-beta assets, leaving a premium
for those willing to lever the low-beta ones — but that premium is **the rent on the leverage**. Charge
the rent and the premium goes with it. This is the same lesson as [Study 30 House-Edge](../../30-house-edge/):
a strategy that "beats the market" only after you assume free borrowing isn't beating the market.

## …and it has decayed

| | gross BAB Sharpe |
|---|---|
| 1999–2012 | **0.70** |
| 2013–on | **0.28** |

The cleanest years for BAB were the early ones; post-publication (Frazzini & Pedersen 2014) the gross
edge more than halved — the McLean–Pontiff fade on top of the financing problem.

## The honest takeaway

Betting against beta is a `WEAK` real tilt that, on a tradable ETF cross-section, **doesn't even beat
the market gross** and needs ~3× leverage to be market-neutral — so realistic financing makes it a
`MIRAGE`. The "low-risk free lunch" is `BUSTED`: you pay for it in borrow. (A caveat held openly: a
finer single-stock universe gives BAB more beta dispersion to work with than 13 ETFs; the *mechanism* —
the edge is the leverage rent — is what generalises, and it is what kills the headline.)
